nodes.description: Two damaged copies of MFN2, either homozygous or compound heterozygous. Reported configurations span the range: homozygosity for a missense allele in a consanguineous family, homozygosity for a novel allele in a sporadic child, compound heterozygosity for a deletion and a missense allele, and compound heterozygosity for a semidominant missense allele (p.R250W) with a nonsense allele (p.R476*). The last of these is the informative one, because the two alleles are known to behave differently on their own.

evidence.reference_title: Severe early-onset axonal neuropathy with homozygous and compound heterozygous MFN2 mutations.

evidence.reference_title: Mutational mechanisms in MFN2-related neuropathy: compound heterozygosity for recessive and semidominant mutations.
evidence.snippet: We describe a 49-year-old woman with CMT5 associated with compound heterozygosity for two MFN2 variants, one already reported missense mutation (c.748C>T, p.R250W) and a novel nonsense sequence change (c.1426C>T, p.R476*).

evidence.reference_title: Autosomal recessive MFN2-related Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease with diaphragmatic weakness: Case report and literature review.
evidence.snippet: A review of the literature reveals that sporadic and familial cases of compound heterozygous or homozygous pathogenic MFN2 variants have been infrequently described, which indicates that MFN2 can also be inherited in a recessive manner.

genetic_context.description: Zygosity varies between reported patients - homozygous in some families, compound heterozygous in others - so no single zygosity value describes the entity and the slot is left unset rather than asserting one family's configuration for all.

nodes.description: Rapidly progressive diaphragmatic paresis requiring tracheostomy and mechanical ventilation in a seven-month-old compound heterozygote. The reporting authors present it as a finding not typically associated with MFN2 variants and as an addition to the phenotype of the recessive form specifically.

evidence.reference_title: Autosomal recessive MFN2-related Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease with diaphragmatic weakness: Case report and literature review.

nodes.description:
This node is the entity's defining mechanistic claim and the reason it is a separate disease from its dominant sibling rather than simply a severe version of it. The determinant of disease is the proportion of mitofusin-2 in the cell that is dysfunctional, not the number of mutated alleles.
The evidence for that is a natural experiment. A nonsense allele carried alone is phenotypically silent - no clinical and no electrophysiological neuropathy - so removing half the protein does nothing. A semidominant missense allele carried alone produces a mild, almost subclinical neuropathy, because roughly half the protein is dysfunctional and half is normal. The same missense allele in trans with the nonsense allele produces severe disease, because now essentially all the mitofusin-2 the cell makes is the dysfunctional kind. And two dysfunctional alleles - the homozygous and compound-heterozygous missense patients - give the severe early-onset picture.
The threshold framing is a synthesis of those observations rather than a measured quantity; no study has titrated mutant against wild-type mitofusin-2 in patient neurons.

evidence.reference_title: Mutational mechanisms in MFN2-related neuropathy: compound heterozygosity for recessive and semidominant mutations.

nodes.description: Mitofusin-2 is a transmembrane GTPase of the mitochondrial outer membrane whose job is to tether and fuse adjacent mitochondria, and so to shape the large connected networks that mitochondria form inside cells. Dysfunctional mitofusin-2 breaks that step. One reported homozygous allele shows how directly: an in-frame deletion removing the proline-rich domain and the first transmembrane domain was predicted by modelling to insert into the outer membrane in a drastically altered topology, and the corresponding fibroblasts contained mitochondria tethered to one another but unable to complete fusion.
nodes.id: Failure of Mitochondrial Outer Membrane Fusion

evidence.reference_title: Mitofusin 2 Dysfunction and Disease in Mice and Men.
evidence.snippet: During the intervening period much has been learned about MFN2 functioning in mitochondrial fusion, calcium signaling, and quality control, and the consequences of these MFN2 activities on cell metabolism, fitness, and development.

nodes.description: Without fusion the network disintegrates. In fibroblasts from a fetus homozygous for an MFN2 deletion, three independent methods - fluorescence imaging, electron microscopy and time-lapse recording - showed a sharply altered network with clumped mitochondria and clusters that were tethered to one another but could not fuse. That last detail is mechanistically specific: the tethering step is preserved and the fusion step is not, which localises the defect within mitofusin-2's own reaction rather than to a failure of mitochondria to meet.

evidence.reference_title: Homozygous MFN2 variants causing severe antenatal encephalopathy with clumped mitochondria.
evidence.snippet: Fetus fibroblasts, investigated by fluorescent cell imaging, electron microscopy and time-lapse recording, showed a sharp alteration of the mitochondrial network, with clumped mitochondria and clusters of tethered mitochondria unable to fuse.

nodes.description: Gait problems are the usual presenting complaint of severe early-onset axonal neuropathy and are the feature that typically brings a child to attention before the diagnosis is made.

nodes.description: Reduced delivery of mitochondria along axons to the distal terminals that depend on them. This node is deliberately hedged and kept separate from quality control because its evidence is weaker: the same 2020 review examines the evidence for and against a regulatory role of mitofusins in mitochondrial transport and treats it as an open question, and states that the central mechanism linking mitochondrial abnormalities to dying-back of peripheral nerves is largely unmet. It names a candidate step and does not claim it is proven.

evidence.reference_title: Mitofusin 2 Dysfunction and Disease in Mice and Men.
evidence.snippet: Evidence for and against a regulatory role of mitofusins in mitochondrial transport is reviewed, nagging questions defined, and implications on mitochondrial fusion, quality control, and neuronal degeneration discussed.

nodes.description: Fusion competence is how a cell decides which mitochondria to keep: organelles that can fuse are retained in the network, and those that cannot are sequestered and cleared by mitophagy. Losing mitofusin-2 therefore does more than fragment the network - it disrupts that sorting step. A 2020 review proposes this as the reason MFN2 dysfunction preferentially affects peripheral nerve.

evidence.reference_title: Mitofusin 2 Dysfunction and Disease in Mice and Men.
evidence.snippet: Here, a different perspective of why, in humans, MFN2 dysfunction preferentially impacts peripheral nerves is provided based on recent insights into its role in determining whether individual mitochondria will be fusion-competent and retained within the cell, or are fusion-impaired, sequestered, and eliminated by mitophagy.

nodes.description:
The clinical disease is a progressive dying-back degeneration of the longest peripheral motor and sensory axons - the arm and leg nerves - producing distal weakness and sensory loss that ascends over time. In the biallelic form the process starts in infancy or early childhood rather than in the second or third decade, progresses to gait failure and often to wheelchair dependence, and reaches respiratory muscle later.
Why peripheral nerve is the tissue that fails is the standing unanswered question of MFN2 biology, and this entry does not answer it. A 2020 review states directly that the challenge of defining the central mechanism linking mitochondrial abnormalities to progressive dying-back of peripheral arm and leg nerves is largely unmet.

evidence.reference_title: MFN2 Hereditary Motor and Sensory Neuropathy.
evidence.snippet: Symptomatic treatment relies on special shoes and/or ankle/foot orthoses to correct foot drop and aid walking; surgery as needed for severe pes cavus; forearm crutches, canes, wheelchairs as needed for mobility; exercise as tolerated; acetaminophen or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents for musculoskeletal pain; treatment of neuropathic pain with tricyclic antidepressants or drugs such as carbamazepine or gabapentin.

evidence.reference_title: MFN2 Hereditary Motor and Sensory Neuropathy.
evidence.snippet: MFN2-HMSN is characterized by more severe involvement of the lower extremities than the upper extremities, distal upper-extremity involvement as the neuropathy progresses, more prominent motor deficits than sensory deficits, and normal (>42 m/s) or only slightly decreased nerve conduction velocities (NCVs). Postural tremor is common.

nodes.description:
Fibroblasts from the homozygous fetus showed deficiencies of multiple respiratory chain complexes with complex I most severely affected - and, importantly, without mitochondrial DNA instability. The absence of an mtDNA lesion matters, because MFN2 sits in a group of genes (with OPA1 and POLG) where mtDNA depletion or deletion is a common downstream mechanism; here the bioenergetic defect follows from the disordered network directly rather than through genome damage.
This is a single fibroblast study in the most severe reported genotype, so it is curated as a cellular observation rather than as an established feature of the entity.
nodes.id: Respiratory Chain Deficiency in Patient Fibroblasts
